title: Core Concepts Overview
passage_text: The demo domain rests on three core concepts: definition, scope, and correct terminology. A strong explanation names each concept precisely, uses the agreed terminology rather than informal paraphrase, and states how the concepts relate to one another rather than listing them in isolation.

title: Terminology Cheat Sheet
passage_text: Common terminology slips include swapping 'concept' for 'idea' where precision matters, and describing a definition without stating its scope. When explaining a concept, always pair the definition with the boundary of what it does and does not cover.

title: Worked Technique Walkthrough
passage_text: Applying the demo technique has four steps. Step 1: identify the sample problem's inputs. Step 2: select the matching technique variant for those inputs - this is the step most students get wrong, usually by picking the variant that matches the output instead of the input. Step 3: apply the technique and record intermediate results. Step 4: check the result against the expected shape of the answer.

title: Technique Application Checklist
passage_text: Before submitting an applied-technique answer, check: did you name which variant of the technique you used, did you show step 2's variant-selection reasoning explicitly, and does your final answer match the input's units and scale.

title: Trade-off Evaluation Framework
passage_text: A critical evaluation names at least one trade-off explicitly: what does the proposed solution gain, and what does it give up to gain it. A discussion that only lists strengths, or only lists weaknesses, has not evaluated a trade-off - it has to compare both sides of the same decision.

title: Worked Trade-off Example
passage_text: Example: a faster technique variant trades accuracy for speed. A thoughtful evaluation states this directly - 'this variant is faster because it approximates step 2, at the cost of some accuracy' - rather than praising the speed alone without naming what was given up for it.

title: Advanced Concepts Overview
passage_text: Advanced demo methods build on the core concepts by adding context-sensitivity: the same method can behave differently depending on the scale of the problem. A strong explanation states which regime the method is operating in before describing its behaviour, rather than describing the method in the abstract.

title: Advanced Terminology Notes
passage_text: At the advanced level, precision matters more: 'method' and 'technique' are not interchangeable, and neither is 'regime' and 'scenario'. State the regime explicitly before naming the method that applies to it.

title: Advanced Technique Walkthrough
passage_text: Applying an advanced demo technique to a complex problem has five steps: decompose the problem into sub-problems, select a technique variant per sub-problem, apply each variant, recombine the intermediate results, and validate the recombined answer against the original problem's constraints. Most errors happen at the recombination step, where students forget to re-check the combined answer against the original constraints.

title: Advanced Application Checklist
passage_text: Before submitting an advanced applied-technique answer, check: did you decompose the problem explicitly, did you name a variant for each sub-problem, and did you re-validate the recombined answer against every original constraint, not just the first one.

title: Advanced Trade-off Framework
passage_text: An advanced critical evaluation compares trade-offs across the whole solution, not just one step: what is gained and given up at each stage, and whether those trade-offs compound or cancel out across the full pipeline. Evaluating only the final step misses trade-offs made earlier that shaped what the final step could achieve.

title: Advanced Trade-off Example
passage_text: Example: decomposing a problem into more sub-problems increases accuracy per sub-problem but increases recombination risk. A thoughtful evaluation names both effects and states which one dominates for the given problem size, rather than evaluating only the accuracy gain.
